title: Cascades
setting: a dam upstream of a town

post.author: u/scarrow_carparks_morwyn
post.title: I'm the night attendant for my town's six car parks. The plate store said healthy at 23:04. Not one barrier lifted by itself until 23:38.

blocks.text: I'm Morwyn, night attendant for the six car parks of Scarrow, a valley town under the Lunsdale dam. From my desk I watch every exit's camera and help button.

Each exit barrier reads the number plate, and the check goes down a chain. The barrier asks the computer that runs all six car parks, the car-park server. That asks a program that knows who has a season pass or booking, the permit service. That asks the list of every plate and its permit, the plate store. Each link in the chain is a layer.

Each layer waits up to 1 second for an answer: its timeout. If none comes, it asks again, up to three more times. Asking again is a retry. Nobody tells the layer below that the one above has given up.

One question to the store is a lookup. It answers lookups one at a time, first come, first served, about 100 a second. Every night at 23:00 it rebuilds its list of where each plate sits, its index, like a book's. For those four minutes each lookup reads the whole list: half a second each.
The store has a busy switch: when its line is too long to answer in time, it can turn a lookup away at once. It's off. Nobody had ever seen a line.
Shows at the Thrumley Arena end by 22:30, and the crowd is gone by 22:50. At 23:00 my other car parks see a car a minute each. Nobody noticed the rebuild.
On Saturday the band played late. At 23:00 a sold-out crowd left: 3,000 cars in 20 minutes, 2.5 a second, through the arena's exits.
At 23:00:04 the station barrier refused a car. The station has no concert traffic.

Quentin, the council's systems man, worked it out in steps. 2.5 cars a second met a store answering two. A line formed, and lookups waited a second or more. The permit service gave up and asked again; so did the server, and the barrier, while every try below kept going. One plate could become 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 lookups. From 23:00:10 the arena alone sent 160 a second.

At 23:04 the rebuild finished. Every few seconds the server asks the store "are you up, is your index built?" That quick test, its health check, said healthy from then on. But 38,434 lookups waited in its line, and more came than it could answer. By their event plan, stewards lifted each arena barrier by key. I lifted the other five from my desk.
The crowd was gone by 23:20. A new lookup waited almost 17 minutes. At 23:38:00 the station barrier lifted by itself. 3,189 cars had been refused.
Quentin pulled the store's log for one season pass at the station. Each line: when it was asked, the plate, the try number at barrier, server and permit service, the wait, and the answer:

23:30:00  HL68 RWT  1.1.1  7m31s  permit ok
23:30:01  HL68 RWT  2.1.1  7m30s  permit ok
23:30:01  HL68 RWT  1.2.1  7m30s  permit ok
...
23:30:09  HL68 RWT  4.4.4  7m22s  permit ok
64 lookups

blocks.title: FRAMED ABOVE MY DESK, FROM GRANDAD'S YEARS AT THE DAM
items: A DAM DOES NOT FAIL IN ONE STORM.
IT FAILS WHEN WATER COMES IN FASTER THAN IT CAN LEAVE.
WHEN IT GOES, EVERYTHING DOWNSTREAM GOES WITH IT.

blocks.text: Sixty-four times the store found her permit, seven minutes after every layer had given up. Every layer did exactly what its settings said. What should Quentin change before the next show?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: What you saw has a name: a cascading failure, one slow part taking down parts that never touched it, and growing by feeding itself. Three sums first. How many lookups can one plate read become, and how many a second at 2.5 cars? Against what the store can answer, which way does its line move? And below how many cars a second would 64 lookups each fit under 100? Then two questions about time. At 23:20, how many lookups in that line still had anybody waiting for the answer? And what does your health check ask that a lookup in the line never has to wait for?

replies.author: u/scarrow_carparks_morwyn
replies.text: Quentin did the sums. 2.5 cars x 64 = 160 lookups a second against 100, so the line grew by about 60 a second until 23:20, when it held 101,212. Below about 1.5 cars a second, 1.5 x 64 = 96 would have fitted, but the crowd never got that low until it was gone. Of the night's 204,141 lookups, 204,092 were answered after the layer that asked had given up. And the health check never joins the line: it asks whether the store is running and its index is built, and both were true.

comments.author: u/capacity_is_the_answer_ermintrude
comments.text: Capacity is the answer. A store that can take 200 a second would never have drowned: 160 fits under 200 with room to spare. Retries are how a system survives a blip, and taking them out turns every hiccup into a refused car. Buy the bigger store and keep the retries.

comments.author: u/just_move_it_truda
comments.text: The rebuild ran at 23:00 on a show night. Put it at 04:00, when the arena has been dark for hours. No slow minutes, no line, no storm. It's one line in a schedule.

reply.prompt: The Thrumley Arena has another sold-out show next month. What should Quentin change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Double the plate store to 200 lookups a second, so it keeps up with a concert crowd.
options.verdict: Fine tonight, not at a bigger show
options.part2: Quentin tried it in the sim first. A store twice as fast is twice as fast during the rebuild too, 4 lookups a second against the crowd's 2.5, so no line ever formed: not one car refused, and HL68 RWT needed one lookup. The council paid for it. Then the arena booked a festival twice the size for September, 5 cars a second. Quentin replayed that in the sim: 5 x 64 = 320 lookups a second against 200. 6,173 cars refused and the barriers back only at 23:36:50, the same night as Saturday with bigger numbers. He took the festival date to the council before it came.
options.senior: More capacity moves the cliff; it doesn't remove it. While three layers each retry on a timeout, a slow spell turns every car into 64 lookups, so a store of 200 a second holds only about 3 cars a second in a storm, and the next bigger crowd tips it over. Capacity is still worth buying for real growth, but size it for the work callers need, not for the work retries invent, and remove the multiplier first.

options.text: Raise every layer's timeout to 5 s, so slow answers count as answers, not failures.
options.part2: Quentin set every timeout to 5 seconds and replayed Saturday in the sim. The storm came later: the first refusal at 23:00:34 instead of 23:00:04. Then it was the same night. The line still grew to 96,775 lookups, 3,149 cars were refused, and the barriers came back at 23:37:30, thirty seconds sooner. Each refused driver now sat 20 seconds at the barrier before it gave up instead of 4, and HL68 RWT's 64 lookups were spread over 45 seconds instead of 9. He put the timeouts back.
options.senior: A longer timeout only changes how long each layer waits before it multiplies the work. Once the line is longer than the timeout, every lookup fails anyway, each layer still retries, and the store still works for callers who have gone; meanwhile every waiting request holds its place longer. Nested timeouts should shrink as you go down, the caller's remaining time passed along, so no layer works on a request nobody will wait for.

options.text: Retry only at the barrier, and let the plate store turn away extra work at once.
options.part2: Quentin set the server and the permit service to ask once, kept the barrier's four tries, and turned the busy switch on: the store now turns away at once any lookup it could not answer within a second. He replayed Saturday in the sim. The rebuild still left two lookups a second for 2.5 cars, so 138 cars were refused between 23:00 and 23:04 and lifted by hand, and the store turned away 554 lookups. But nothing piled up behind them. At 23:03:57 a barrier lifted by itself, and from then on every one did. HL68 RWT needed one lookup. At the next show the night log had two lines about the barriers, both before 23:04.
options.senior: Retry at one layer, usually the top one, which knows whether anyone is still waiting; layers below ask once and pass the failure up, so one plate costs at most 4 lookups, not 64. Then let the part that is overloaded refuse extra work early and cheaply, before it spends effort, so whatever it does accept is answered in time. Add a retry budget so retries stay a small share of traffic, and make the health check ask the real path. The four slow minutes remain a cost, so the rebuild still belongs off show nights.

options.text: Move the store's nightly index rebuild to 04:00, when no crowd ever leaves a show.
options.verdict: Tonight's trigger gone, the storm kept
options.part2: Quentin moved the rebuild to 04:00. In the sim, Saturday with no slow spell is clean: not one car refused. Then he tried a 30 second hiccup at 23:10, the kind any computer has now and then, during the same crowd. The arena's 2.5 cars a second met 2 answers a second for half a minute, the retries multiplied, and the store never caught up while the crowd lasted: 1,586 cars refused and the barriers back only at 23:27:24. Thirty seconds of slow cost seventeen minutes of shut barriers.
options.senior: Moving the rebuild removes Saturday's trigger, not the cause. The cause is a system that multiplies work when it slows down and keeps doing work nobody is waiting for, so any short slow spell under load, a hiccup, a backup, a busy neighbour, sets off the same storm. Plan for the slow minute you didn't schedule; that is what retry limits and load shedding are for.

sim.title: Replay Saturday night at Scarrow's car parks
sim.lede: You're Quentin, at 22:58:00 on Saturday. From 23:00:00 to 23:20:00 the arena sends one car every 0.4 seconds, 2.5 a second; each of the other five car parks sends one car a minute. Each barrier asks the car-park server, which asks the permit service, which asks the plate store: every layer waits up to its timeout and tries again, up to 3 more times, and nobody tells the layer below to stop. The store answers one lookup at a time, first come, first served: 100 a second, but 2 a second during the index rebuild from 23:00:00 to 23:04:00. It works through every lookup in its line, even one whose caller has gone. A car whose barrier gives up is lifted by hand. Set the exit rate, the slow spell, the timeout, the retries, which layers retry, the busy switch and the store's size, then play to 23:45:00.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Next minute until 23:01:00, as built. From 23:00:10 the arena's cars make 160 lookups a second against room for 2. Play on: at 23:04:00 the health check says healthy, yet every car park is shut. Go to the end: HL68 RWT looked up 64 times from 23:30:00 to 23:30:09, barriers back at 23:38:00. Now each idea. Store 200: nothing refused; then 5 cars a second: back at 23:36:50. Timeout 5 s: back at 23:37:30. Slow spell none, then the 23:10 hiccup: back at 23:27:24. Barrier only, with the busy switch on: 138 refused, all before 23:04, back at 23:03:57.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in Scarrow was slow for more than four minutes. Three layers each retried on a 1 second timeout, so a slow store turned 2.5 cars a second into 160 lookups a second against room for 100. The line grew faster than the store could empty it, and the store spent half an hour answering questions nobody was waiting for, while its health check said healthy.

steps.title: Four slow minutes met a crowd.
steps.text: During the rebuild the store answers one lookup in half a second, two a second. On every earlier night that was plenty: about five cars a minute across the town, each answered in half a second, well inside the 1 second timeout. On Saturday 2.5 cars a second arrived at 23:00. What went wrong, step by step: each second half a lookup more arrived than the store could answer, so a line formed; within seconds a lookup waited longer than the timeout; then the retries began, and the line went from slow to hopeless.

steps.title: Every layer retried, so the work multiplied.
steps.text: A retry at one layer is polite. Retries at three layers multiply. The barrier tries 4 times; each try makes the server try 4 times; each of those makes the permit service ask the store 4 times: 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 lookups for one plate, asked over 9 seconds. Because every layer had the same 1 second timeout, an inner retry could never answer the layer above in time: by the moment the permit service asked again, the server had already given up on it. So 60 of the 64 could never help anyone. 2.5 cars a second became 160 lookups a second, a retry storm. Google's SRE book gives the same sum: 3 retries at three layers is 64 attempts on the database for one user action.

steps.title: The store worked for callers who had gone, so the end of the cause wasn't the end.
steps.text: The store answered strictly in order and could not tell which lookups were still wanted. At 23:04 it was fast again, 100 a second, but 38,434 lookups were waiting and 160 more arrived every second, so the line kept growing to 101,212 at 23:20. Every lookup that joined it waited longer than any layer would, failed, and was retried, which kept the line full. That is the feedback loop that makes a cascading failure: slow answers cause retries, retries cause slower answers. It only stops when the work coming in falls below what the store can do, under about 1.5 cars a second here, and then the store still has to empty the line. The crowd was gone at 23:20; the line took until 23:38. The five quiet car parks shared the same store, so they drowned with the arena: 204,092 of 204,141 answers that night went to nobody.

steps.title: The health check asked the cheap question.
steps.text: A health check (s2e02) is only as good as its question. Scarrow's asks "are you running, is your index built?" Both were true from 23:04, so it said healthy while a real lookup waited 17 minutes. Google's book separates the two: is the program running at all, and can it answer this kind of request right now? A check that sends one real lookup through the real line, and fails if the answer is slow, would have shown red until 23:38.

steps.title: Retry at one layer; let the busy part turn work away.
steps.text: The fix has two halves. First, only the top layer retries: the barrier keeps its 4 tries and the layers below ask once and pass a failure straight up, so one plate costs at most 4 lookups. Second, load shedding: the store turns away at once any lookup it could not answer within a second, with a quick "busy". That costs it nothing, so whatever it accepts is answered in time and no line of dead work builds up. Its cousin is backpressure (s4e15): telling the senders to slow down rather than letting the line grow. A retry budget, retries kept to a small share of first tries, keeps even the top layer honest. In the sim, 138 cars are still refused during the four slow minutes, and every barrier works again from 23:03:57.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next show. The barrier tries up to 4 times, 1 second apart, and asks the car-park server. The server asks the permit service once. The permit service asks the plate store once. The plate store turns away at once any lookup it can't answer within 1 second. In the sim, 138 cars are refused during the rebuild and every barrier lifts by itself from 23:03:57.

nodes.meta: turns away what it can't do in 1 s

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next show. Only the barrier retries, so one plate costs at most 4 lookups; the store turns away at once what it can't answer within a second. In the sim, the four slow minutes still cost 138 cars lifted by hand, and from 23:03:57 every barrier lifts by itself.

fix.title: The fix: retry at one layer, and let the busy part turn work away
fix.text: Set the car-park server and the permit service to ask once and pass any failure straight up; keep the barrier's 4 tries, since the barrier knows whether a car is still waiting. Turn the store's busy switch on, so it turns away at once any lookup it could not answer within a second. Give the barrier a retry budget, so its retries stay a small share of its first tries even on a bad night. Change the health check to send one real lookup through the real line. And still move the rebuild off show nights: four slow minutes are a cost even when they no longer spread. Check it in the sim: 138 refused, all before 23:04, every barrier lifting by itself from 23:03:57, HL68 RWT answered with one lookup.

limits: Load shedding decides who waits; it doesn't make room. During the rebuild the store can still answer only two lookups a second, so 138 cars still needed a steward or the desk. The rebuild still belongs at a quiet hour.
Retrying at one layer only helps if every layer below fails fast and says so. A layer that hangs, or a new caller such as an app that adds its own retries, brings the multiplying back.
Turning work away moves the problem to the caller: someone must handle "busy" sensibly, here a steward or the attendant. And shedding needs a good estimate of what the store can answer in time.

explain.seniorTake: Retries are a loan against the part you're calling: each one spends its time to raise your chance. One layer borrowing is fine. Every layer borrowing on the same slow part multiplies the debt, and the part that is slow is the one asked to pay it. So decide where retries live, usually at the top, which knows if anyone is still waiting, and make every layer below fail fast and pass the failure up. Give retries a budget. Shrink timeouts as you go down the chain, or pass the caller's remaining time along, so nobody works on a request that has already been abandoned. At the busy part, refuse early and cheaply: a quick "busy" costs nothing, while queued dead work can keep a system broken long after its cause has gone. Then test the real path in your health checks, because a check that skips the line will call a drowning system healthy. And ask what happens when a slow minute meets your busiest minute, because it will.

realWorld.title: AWS, December 2021: retries that would not back off
realWorld.text: AWS's summary of the 7 December 2021 event in its Northern Virginia region says an automated scaling activity "triggered an unexpected behavior from a large number of clients inside the internal network", causing "a large surge of connection activity that overwhelmed the networking devices between the internal network" and the main AWS network. Delays then led to "even more connection attempts and retries", and "a latent issue prevented these clients from adequately backing off during this event."

realWorld.title: AWS, December 2021: hard to see from inside
realWorld.text: The congestion also hit AWS's own tools: it "impaired their ability to find the source of congestion and resolve it", and "the impact on internal monitoring limited our ability to understand the problem." Among the changes: "We immediately disabled the scaling activities that triggered this event."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: what a cascading failure is
realWorld.text: "A cascading failure is a failure that grows over time as a result of positive feedback." The chapter adds that it is often hard to escape: in its example, "dropping the load to 9,000 QPS will almost certainly not stop the crashes", and "the request rate would need to drop to about 1,000 QPS in order for the system to stabilize and recover." Scarrow's store needed the crowd gone, not just thinner.

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: retries at every layer, 64 attempts
realWorld.text: The book's own sum: "If the database can't service requests because it's overloaded, and the backend, frontend, and JavaScript layers all issue 3 retries (4 attempts), then a single user action may create 64 attempts (4^3) on the database." Its advice is to "avoid amplifying retries by issuing retries at multiple levels".

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: retry budgets
realWorld.text: "Limit retries per request." And: "Consider having a server-wide retry budget. For example, only allow 60 retries per minute in a process, and if the retry budget is exceeded, don't retry; just fail the request."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: load shedding and failing early
realWorld.text: "Load shedding drops some proportion of load by dropping traffic as the server approaches overload conditions." And: "When overloaded at either the frontend or backend layers, fail early and cheaply." On deadlines: "the client doesn't care what work the server does after the deadline has passed", so servers "should employ deadline propagation."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: two kinds of health check
realWorld.text: "Process health checking ("is this binary responding at all?") and service health checking ("is this binary able to respond to this class of requests right now?") are two conceptually distinct operations." Scarrow's check was the first kind.

asked: How can retries make an outage worse?
Where should retries live in a call chain?
interview.answer: Retries make an outage worse when the thing being retried is slow because it is overloaded. Every retry is more work for the part that is already struggling, and if several layers each retry, the work multiplies: three layers with 3 retries each turn one user action into 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 attempts, the figure Google's SRE book uses. Worse, if the slow part answers in order and can't tell who has given up, it spends its time on requests nobody is waiting for, so it stays broken after the original cause has gone. I'd put retries in one place, usually the top of the chain or the client, which knows whether anyone still wants the answer, and make every layer below fail fast and pass the error up. I'd cap retries with a retry budget, use backoff with jitter, shrink timeouts down the chain or propagate deadlines, and never retry something that isn't safe to repeat. Load shedding is the overloaded part refusing extra work early and cheaply, with a quick error, instead of queueing it, so whatever it does accept is answered in time; it's the server-side partner to backpressure, where you tell senders to slow down. And I'd make health checks exercise the real request path, because a check that only asks whether the process is up will report healthy while requests drown. The story I'd tell: a car-park system whose three layers each retried 3 times on a 1 second timeout; a four-minute index rebuild met a concert crowd, 2.5 cars a second became 160 lookups a second against a store that answers 100, and barriers stayed shut for half an hour after the store said healthy. Retrying only at the barrier and letting the store turn work away kept it to the four slow minutes.

atWork: Look for chains where each service retries the next: an app that calls a gateway, which calls a service, which calls a database, each with its own retry setting chosen by a different team. It is a common pattern, and it hides on good days because nothing fails. Multiply the tries at every layer: that is how many requests one user action can become at the bottom when the bottom is slow. Then check four things. Which layer is meant to retry, and do the others fail fast and pass the error up? Is there a retry budget? Does the busiest part refuse extra work quickly, or queue it forever? And does its health check send a real request through the real path, or only ask whether the process is up? Loadout L6 builds exactly this: a retry-storm scenario that collapses without backoff and survives with it. Standards: if your company is pursuing SOC 2 availability, criterion A1.1 expects it to maintain, monitor and evaluate current processing capacity and use of system components; retries that multiply load and health checks that miss it are that kind of capacity risk, so measure them now rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your shop's app calls an API gateway, which calls the orders service, which calls the database. Each one retries a failed call 3 times with a 2 s timeout. During a sale the database had a two-minute slow spell. It has been fast for twenty minutes and its health check says healthy, yet orders are still failing and the database is busier than at any time in the sale. What is going on, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Retries at every layer multiply: one order can become 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 database calls, so a slow spell turns into a storm
The database is still working through calls whose callers have given up, so it stays overloaded after the cause has gone
Retry at one layer only, with a budget, and let the database shed load by refusing extra work fast

recall.model: It's a retry storm, and a cascading failure. When the database slowed, each layer timed out and retried, and because three layers each retry 3 times, one order could multiply into 64 database calls. The database answers in order and can't tell which callers have given up, so it is still working through a backlog of calls nobody is waiting for; every new call joins the back, times out and is retried, which keeps it overloaded long after the slow spell ended. The health check passes because it only asks whether the database is up. I'd retry in one layer only, the app or the gateway, with a retry budget and backoff with jitter, make the services below fail fast and pass errors up, let the database shed load by refusing extra work quickly, and make the health check send a real query.

recall.prompt: Three layers each try a call up to 4 times (1 try and 3 retries) on a 1 second timeout, and every call times out. Cars arrive at 2.5 a second. How many lookups a second reach the store once the storm is in full swing?
options: 10, since only the barrier's 4 tries count
160, since each car can become 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 lookups
2.5, since each car is one plate
recall.why: The tries multiply, they don't add: each of the barrier's 4 tries makes 4 server tries, and each of those makes 4 lookups, 64 in all. At 2.5 cars a second that is 160 lookups a second, against a store that answers 100.

recall.prompt: The plate store's health check asks "are you running, is your index built?" At 23:20 a real lookup waits almost 17 minutes. What does the health check say, and why?
options: Unhealthy, because the store is overloaded
Healthy, because the check never waits in the line that real lookups wait in
Nothing, because a health check times out under load
Healthy, because health checks only run once an hour
recall.why: The check asks a cheap question the store can answer without joining its line, and both answers were true. Google's SRE book calls this process health against service health: is it running, and can it answer this kind of request right now? Only a check that sends a real lookup through the real line would have shown the drowning.

recall.prompt: The store can answer 100 lookups a second, and during a slow spell lookups pile up. Which change lets it recover as soon as the slow spell ends?
options: Turn away at once any lookup it can't answer in time, so no line of dead work builds up
Answer every lookup in order, however long the line gets
Give the store a longer line so nothing is ever turned away
Raise every caller's timeout so more answers count
recall.why: Load shedding refuses extra work early and cheaply. Refusing costs the store almost nothing, so whatever it accepts is answered in time, and when the slow spell ends there is no backlog of answers for callers who have gone. A longer line or longer timeouts only store up more work.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Only the barriers retry now, and the store's busy switch is on. The spring shows each had a few refusals during the rebuild and none after 23:04. In July the council launched a parking app: you can extend your stay from your phone, and it asks the permit service directly. Its makers set it to repeat any failed request 5 times, straight away. On the first show night with the app, the store turned away far more lookups than in spring, and about three times as many cars needed a steward between 23:00 and 23:04.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did a phone app make the barriers worse, and what should the app and the store do?

keyIdeas.idea: The app is a new caller with its own retries; its instant repeats add load at exactly the moment the store is turning work away
The app should back off with jitter and keep to a retry budget, treating busy as a signal to wait
The store should shed by priority: keep the barriers' lookups and turn away the app's first

coldCase.model: The app is a new caller with its own retries, and it repeats every failed request immediately, 6 tries in a row. During the rebuild the store turns work away, so each busy answer comes straight back as five more requests: the retries multiply again, just from a new direction, and the barriers' own lookups have to compete with them for two answers a second. The app should back off with jitter and keep to a retry budget, treating a busy answer as a reason to wait, not to ask again at once. And the store should shed by priority: a car at a barrier is waiting now, someone extending their stay can wait a minute, so keep the barriers' lookups and turn away the app's first.
